# AI & Economics of Science Papers — 2026-08-01

## 1. Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation [AI for Science]

**Authors:** Lennart Meincke, Karan Girotra, Gideon Nave, Christian Terwiesch, Karl T. Ulrich
**Date:** July 30, 2026
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27553
**Summary:** The authors compare pools of new-product ideas generated by university students in a pre-LLM design course against ideas generated by GPT-4 under zero-shot and few-shot prompting, scoring quality via market-research purchase-intent measures and human-rated novelty. AI-generated ideas beat human ideas on average purchase intent and were seven times more likely to land in the top decile of quality, even though they scored lower on novelty and clustered more closely together in idea space. The results suggest LLMs can already outperform trained humans at generating commercially promising ideas in bulk, even as their convergent, less-diverse output raises questions about whether AI-driven ideation narrows the range of solutions explored.

## 2. Opaque Epistemic Mediation: How LLM Deployment Configurations Shape the Validation of Pseudo-Science [Peer Review & Publication]

**Authors:** Davide Scarso, Hugo Noronha de Almeida, Joaquim Pina
**Date:** July 24, 2026 (v1); revised July 27, 2026
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22513
**Summary:** The authors repeatedly probed four major LLM families (Claude, Grok, GPT, Gemini) across API and web interfaces over several months, asking each to rate the credibility of an ethnonationalist pseudo-scientific framework alongside control claims about mainstream and refuted evolutionary biology. They found Grok's default consumer-facing versions scored the pseudo-science two to five times more credible than every other model, that an undocumented patch abruptly flipped Grok's behavior overnight, and that identical model identifiers gave sharply different answers depending on whether they were queried via API or web. The findings show that an LLM's stance on contested scientific claims is not a fixed property of the model but a volatile function of opaque deployment choices, which the authors argue creates an unaccountable channel for legitimizing pseudo-science at scale.

## 3. Measuring the State of Open Science in Transportation Using Large Language Models [Econ of Science]

**Authors:** Junyi Ji, Ruth Lu, Linda Belkessa, Liming Wang, Silvia Varotto, Yongqi Dong, Nicolas Saunier, Mostafa Ameli, Gregory S. Macfarlane, Bahman Madadi, Cathy Wu
**Date:** January 20, 2026 (v1); revised July 28, 2026
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14429
**Summary:** The authors build an LLM-based pipeline to automatically detect whether papers share code and data, then apply it to 10,724 transportation-research articles published between 2019 and 2024, validating the extraction against hand-coded labels. They find only about 5% of quantitative papers share code and 4% share data, with adoption varying by journal, topic, and region, and crucially find no citation or review-speed advantage for papers that do share. The near-absence of any reward for open-science behavior implies that transparency in this field won't improve without structural pressure from journals and funders, since authors currently have little private incentive to bear the cost.

## 4. Comparative Analysis of Classification Schemes on Major Bibliometric Platforms: A study of Web of Science, Scopus, the Lens, and Dimensions [Peer Review & Publication]

**Authors:** Ophélie Fraisier-Vannier
**Date:** July 28, 2026
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.25499
**Summary:** The paper systematically compares how Web of Science, Scopus, Dimensions, and The Lens classify scholarly output, ranging from expert-curated journal-level taxonomies to AI-driven document-level classification. It documents substantial structural and granularity differences across platforms that can change which papers show up in a given field-level search or bibliometric analysis. Because researchers, funders, and evaluators increasingly rely on these platforms' categories to measure productivity and allocate credit, the mismatch between classification schemes is a hidden source of inconsistency in science-of-science and research-evaluation studies.

## 5. Scientific Knowledge Discovery in the Age of Large Language Models [AI for Science]

**Authors:** Eleni Adamidi, Serafeim Chatzopoulos, Thanasis Vergoulis
**Date:** July 29, 2026
**Source:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26670
**Summary:** This book chapter systematically reviews 34 peer-reviewed studies that use generative LLMs for literature retrieval and screening candidate papers against eligibility criteria, drawn from a Boolean search of 1,589 records in the OpenAIRE Graph. It catalogs which models, adaptation techniques, prompting strategies, ground-truth sources, and evaluation metrics researchers have used to automate these two classically labor-intensive steps of systematic reviewing. The synthesis maps how far LLM-assisted literature discovery has progressed and highlights the lack of standardized evaluation practice across the field, which limits comparability between competing approaches.
